title: The first crib (Greccio, 1223)
hook: Francis sets up a manger with an ox and donkey so people can see

segments.voice: Yesterday, San Damiano, and a crucifix that asked Francis to rebuild. Your line was start with stones. What small thing did you put back together? Day eight hundred seven.

A bundle of hay. An ox. A donkey. A rough wooden feeding trough in a hillside village called Greccio, in the middle of a winter night. People climb up from the farms around with candles and torches, and the woods fill with light and singing. In Celano's telling no one lays a baby in the straw. There's a manger, two animals breathing in the cold, and a small man in a patched habit, overflowing with joy. Francis of Assisi has asked a friend to build this. Today's word is the name people later gave it: the first crib.
screen: `HAY, AN OX, A DONKEY.` → `TORCHES ON A WINTER NIGHT.` → `AN EMPTY MANGER.`

segments.voice: Start with why. Thomas of Celano, who wrote an early life of Francis, says Francis wanted to see with his own eyes how the child of Bethlehem had lain in a manger, with the hardship of it, the ox and the ass standing by. Francis had heard the Christmas story all his life. He wanted the village to see it, not only hear it. The Gospel line he had in mind is Luke's, which in the Douay-Rheims reads: "and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." Then, the animals. They aren't in Luke. They come from the prophet Isaiah: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." Tradition placed those two animals beside the manger, and Francis put real ones there. A dumb beast, the prophet says, knows where its food comes from. Francis wanted people to stand next to one and remember. Next, the Mass. A priest celebrated Mass right over the manger. Francis, who was a deacon and never a priest, sang the Gospel and then preached, and Celano says he called Jesus the child of Bethlehem, saying the word Bethlehem so tenderly it sounded like a lamb's bleat. Celano adds that one man there saw a child lying in the manger as if asleep, and Francis seemed to wake him. Last, what stayed. Celano doesn't call Greccio the first of anything; first is the title tradition gave it later. What Greccio gave was a habit. Catholic homes and parishes still set out a crib in Advent, with an ox and a donkey nearby. A faith you can stand in front of, and see.
screen: `HE WANTED TO SEE IT WITH HIS EYES.` · `THE OX AND ASS COME FROM ISAIAH.` · `MASS SUNG OVER THE MANGER.` · `A HABIT THAT STAYED.` · then, large: `NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set up something visible for faith, or for whatever you hold dear. It can be small. A crucifix moved to where you'll actually pass it. A holy card on the fridge. A candle on the table. A photograph of someone you pray for, or simply love. Choose it now, and if it's in reach, put it in place. Then sit and look at it, the way the people at Greccio looked at an empty manger. If you pray, you can let the sight of it be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
The first crib. The manger, the ox and the donkey Francis set out at Greccio so a village could see the Christmas story. Today's word.
Your line: so they could see. Today, notice one thing in your home that shows what you love without a word, and keep it where people can see it. Day eight hundred seven.

howItsDone: Catholic families and parishes set up a crib, or nativity scene, for Advent and Christmas; some wait until Christmas Eve to lay the figure of the child in the manger.

original.note: Latin: a manger or crib, the word Luke's Gospel uses in the Latin Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first crib is the first nativity scene ever made.
what it means: the night Francis set out a manger, an ox and a donkey at Greccio so a village could see the story, with Mass sung beside it.
what a scholar hears: Celano's account in his first life of Francis, which never calls it the first; that title is tradition's.

notes: Year 1223 appears only in the index title; not spoken.
Index word 'The first crib' kept exactly; the teach says 'first' is tradition's title and that earlier Christmas images and plays existed. Confirm phrasing.

Celano details paraphrased: Francis wanting to see the infant's hardship with bodily eyes; torches and candles; Mass over the manger; Francis as deacon singing the Gospel; 'Bethlehem' spoken like a lamb's bleat; the vision of the child seeming to wake. Confirm each against Celano I, 84–86.
'In the oldest telling, no baby doll': Celano describes an empty manger with a vision of a child; confirm.
Isaiah 1:3 Douay-Rheims wording and 'tradition placed those two animals beside the manger': confirm.
Original: Vulgate Luke 2:7 'in praesepio'; nominative praesepe/praesepium. Confirm form and pronunciation.

Editor: cut the unsourced 'historians note earlier Christmas scenes and plays' claim (teach and trapdoor) in favor of 'Celano doesn't call it the first'; replaced 'no baby doll, no costumes' with what Celano's telling shows; smoothed a myth reveal; removed a stale note.

Second editor pass: cut the unsourced 'nobody in the crowd is acting'; 'can hardly speak for joy' (which clashed with Francis singing the Gospel and preaching) changed to 'overflowing with joy', closer to Celano.
